## 1. Bind client configuration and authority

In the accepted selected checkout, complete
[cluster/release preflight](../install.md#bind-cluster-authority) and
[Prepare the client projections](../maintenance.md#prepare-the-client-projections).
That procedure extracts one reviewed Buster render and produces private new
BuildKit, runtime and node projections from one `registry-clients.v1` contract.
Retain the sanitized origin/reference, render/contract/projection digests and
credential-authority reference, not generated credential-bearing node contents.

Do not hand-edit one client projection to make a failed task pass. Worker
entrypoint regeneration, node installation and effective container-runtime
routing are different actions. In particular, the node example selects no
registry by itself. The source-only node inspector cannot prove effective
containerd routing, DNS, authentication or a pull. Complete
[Install and prove the selected clients](../maintenance.md#install-and-prove-the-selected-clients)
before new runtime deployment or a node change.

For a controlled build, use a new approved attempt-owned output name/tag in the
resolved plan. The build context and Dockerfile must remain inside the admitted
provider repository/scratch boundaries. Protected credential arguments do not
belong in Docker build args; use the selected credential authority. The
provider's default platform is not evidence of the consuming node's platform.
Select and retain the actual allowed platform explicitly when that distinction
matters.

## 2. Run the supported build and retain its result

For a governed project, use the exact compile/start/audit procedure in
[Run a Buster Suite](buster-suite.md#5-submit-and-observe-in-production) with the
same source, platform, project and plan. Do not submit a hand-written remote job
or call BuildKit directly to bypass source attestation, provider admission or
result/evidence import.

The maintained live build **preflight**, when its registered installation and
receipt authority are available, has this separate entry point:

```bash
assert_cluster_binding || exit 126
./scripts/deploy.sh nova-buildkit-preflight
```

Use the selected checkout and bound shell from the linked install procedure.
This command starts real remote work and can publish an image; it is not an
offline validation command. The deployed Nova/Buster token/source key and
external production receipt signing/trust keys must already belong to their
proper authorities. Missing credentials, selected release, worker readiness or
signing authority are stops, not permission to synthesize them.

The preflight owns a new temporary Git fixture, new run and idempotency identity.
It builds an nginx-based page carrying that run ID. Its Dockerfile uses a tagged
upstream base; its successful output digest is exact, but this is not proof of
reproducibility from only the source commit or an unchanged upstream tag.

Require the actual remote status `completed`, gate decision `passed`, one
complete matching imported result/evidence record and no runner cleanup error.
The unsigned result uses `nova-container-build-production-preflight.v4` and
identifies run/job, source/runtime revisions, plan/result/decision digests,
evidence digests and the digest-qualified image. The wrapper then checks the
observed Buster revision and signs/verifies its production receipt before
storing `dist/verification/container-build-production-receipt.json`.
Retain full terminal output and status plus the accepted receipt through the
existing evidence owner; a wrapper failure can occur after the build succeeded.

## 4. Require the consuming-node observation or stop

Publication does not install or run the image. Before a node exercise, its owner
must bind the node identity, OS/architecture/variant, runtime/version, effective
registry/mirror route, CA/auth source and exact digest. The approved procedure
must preserve the existing node configuration, define the reload/restart
boundary and rollback, and isolate an owned test workload from production.

Use that procedure's actual cold-pull control. Evidence must distinguish an
uncached manifest resolution/fetch from a ready Pod that reused local content.
Do not evict shared production images, clear all runtime caches or set a pull
policy and call it proof that every layer was uncached. An `IfNotPresent` start
can use a cache; even a successful digest resolution is not a universal claim
that every layer transferred again.

Observe the exact consuming Pod UID, node, selected container name,
`containerID`, requested immutable image, runtime-reported `imageID` and any
restart. Bind those observations to the retained manifest/platform identity,
then run the owning application's bounded reader for its expected content and
authorized access. The preflight page's expected run text is useful only if the
actual original image and retained run ID are still known; a different image
or generic HTTP 200 cannot close this observation.

The repository's client generator and build preflight supply no complete node
installation/restart/cold-pull/application-reader command sequence. Stop here
when the platform owner has not supplied that versioned procedure and per-node
proof. Name the missing node/runtime, configuration, trust/credential, expected
image/content and cleanup authority in the stop record. Local client generation
or a successful push cannot fill it.

## 5. Bound failure and retry authority

For an approved lab endpoint denial, reuse
[Registry Endpoint Unavailable During BuildKit Push](../diagnose.md#registry-endpoint-unavailable-during-buildkit-push).
Its guarded original Service/consumer identities, bounded fault window, exact
selector restoration and independent mirror observations remain authoritative.
Do not repeat those destructive settings on another registry or translate a
reachability fault into a TLS/credential bypass.

Read the first failed boundary: source/registry admission; BuildKit launch or
build; push; bounded manifest read/hash; evidence import; runner cleanup; or
wrapper signing. The capability distinguishes completed nonzero build output
from launch, deadline, cancellation and verification errors. Do not call an
arbitrary nonzero wrapper status a proved push denial.

An interrupted or failed preflight removes its temporary source/Nova state in
its finalizer and creates new identities on the next call. It has no supported
operator original-state custody/read operation. Therefore a new preflight is
not a retry or reconciliation of a possibly accepted push. Preserve original
stdout/stderr/status, interval, any request/job/image identities and signed or
unsigned receipt. Mark missing original identities unavailable.

Stop new build admission and have the Nova/Buster/registry owners inspect the
original job and intended attempt tag/digest through an authorized read path.
If that supported read/custody path is unavailable, retain the uncertainty and
follow [uncertain external effects](../diagnose.md#lost-responses-and-uncertain-effects).
Do not manually import a result, edit state, rebuild different content under an
old identity or delete a possibly published image to make the uncertainty vanish.

## 6. Cleanup and final decision

Restore the exact fault controls before ending its approved window. Remove only
owned disposable consumer resources through the node/application procedure,
and verify their absence or bounded retained ownership. Dispose of generated
credential-bearing client files through their credential owner; retain sanitized
projection digests and prior configuration for rollback.

The build capability removes its own temporary Docker authentication/metadata
directory; that does not delete a pushed registry image or prove remote layer
cleanup. Registry image/tag retirement and garbage collection require the
registry owner's retention, referenced-manifest inventory and backup contract.
Do not delete shared blobs or active release digests as test cleanup.

Record separate outcomes for build/push, verified manifest/import, cold node
pull, original-image application observation, failure reconciliation and cleanup.
Claim the whole chain only when all required observations agree. Otherwise
retain the exact implemented partial result and named safe stop without
promoting it to a completed node-consumer workflow.

## Before You Start

Run repository proofs from the KubeClaw repository root. Run production
compile, start, audit, and recovery commands from the original KubeClaw checkout
in the Nova installation that owns the pipeline state. Its `package.json`
defines `npm run pipeline`; the project descriptor's `repositoryRoot` separately
selects the source repository. That repository can be elsewhere and does not
need a Nova npm script. Keep the command shell in the original KubeClaw checkout
and use absolute platform, project, graph, and evidence paths.

The [pipeline npm script](https://github.com/datrab/kubeclaw/blob/4dc3ff5829f3298a4d04148216e4e7da9b20c49b/package.json#L42)
loads the [Nova dispatcher](https://github.com/datrab/kubeclaw/blob/3cf7dc4f72c2ae1e0ba4c47cceb08c98f4c70b7f/skills/nova/pipeline.ts#L1-L14).
The [project CLI](https://github.com/datrab/kubeclaw/blob/3cf7dc4f72c2ae1e0ba4c47cceb08c98f4c70b7f/skills/nova/project/cli.ts#L46-L51)
checks the selected project's HEAD and clean working tree with `git -C` before
starting a new run. Compilation does not perform those two source checks.

For a production run, the operator needs permission to start and inspect that
Nova pipeline. The Buster service account, token, source key, and capability credentials remain
service-owned; a project author does not need direct access to them.

Confirm these facts before either path:

- the project is in Git and the revision to test is committed;
- Nova and Buster use compatible pipeline-test-gate contracts;
- the Buster role contains the selected provider and report adapter packages;
- the operator catalogue maps `npm` to an approved executable;
- the project command creates the declared JUnit file inside its workspace;
- Nova can authenticate to the Buster endpoint; and
- Buster has enough state, result, archive, and evidence capacity.

For a repository proof, first complete the canonical
[Locked Dependency Installation](../quickstart.md#locked-dependency-installation),
confirm the checkout is clean, and confirm that the current Node.js version
satisfies `package.json`. The vertical proof also needs a C compiler, GNU `flock`,
`/usr/bin/tar`, and permission to start child processes.

Stop before submission when resolution fails, the source revision is not the
intended committed revision, the Buster readiness endpoint is not ready, or a
required live dependency is absent. Do not use a smaller check to waive one of
these conditions.

Do not use an uncommitted working tree as input. Nova sends a `git archive` of
the committed tree. A local file that is not in that tree cannot appear in the
remote workspace.

## 5. Submit and Observe in Production

There is no separate manual Buster submission command. Compile the project
first. Replace `<platform.json>` with the operator-owned platform file,
`<project.json>` with the project descriptor, and `<new-pipeline.json>` with a
new absolute path that does not exist. Run this command from the original
KubeClaw checkout, with absolute platform and project paths:

```text
npm run pipeline -- \
  --platform "<platform.json>" \
  --project "<project.json>" \
  --compile "<new-pipeline.json>"
```

Stop if compilation does not return `status: compiled`, or if the graph does
not contain the intended Buster quality stage and test scope. Record its
`definitionDigest`, derived `runId`, and completion scope. Compilation checks
registration and grants. It does not contact Buster.

Before starting, check that the repository selected by the descriptor's
`repositoryRoot` has committed HEAD equal to its intended `baseRevision` and a
clean working tree. Stop on either mismatch. Run the start command from the
same original KubeClaw checkout used for compilation:

```text
npm run pipeline -- \
  --platform "<platform.json>" \
  --project "<project.json>"
```

Expected output is one JSON object with `runId`, `status`, `completionScope`,
`acceptanceReadiness`, and stage states. Preserve that object. Exit zero means
the returned pipeline status is `succeeded`; it does not by itself prove human
acceptance or every external live prerequisite.

Nova records dispatch intent before it contacts Buster. Buster verifies source
signature, archive digest, derived job ID, request digest, plan digest, provider
identity, and store capacity before it returns `accepted`.

Observe the states in order: `accepted`, `running`, and one terminal state.
`completed` means that Buster produced a complete result object. It does not
mean that every blocking test passed. Nova must fetch the exact result digest,
verify its identities and receipts, import every referenced evidence digest,
and then calculate the gate decision.

Before audit, complete [Inspect a Run](../operate.md#inspect-a-run) at the
original Nova repository in Bash. Use the original platform path and the run
ID from the retained start command. Confirm that the run owner has exited,
stop new writes to that run and the owning adapter stores, and preserve
verified raw run and adapter copies. Audit can create append locks and truncate
an incomplete journal tail before parsing. Require successful strict parsing
of every copied run journal. Keep rejected raw bytes and stop on copy,
identity, or parse failure. Define the canonical `preserve_run_state` helper
in this shell; do not duplicate or replace it with a storage-opening reader.

If a run is still active, retain its command output and use supported component
or provider observations. Stop before audit when stopped-writer ownership and
preservation cannot be established. Process containment is not a successful
suite result. With all preservation checks complete, audit the returned identity:

```bash
export RUN_CONTROL_PLATFORM="<original-platform.json>"
export RUN_CONTROL_RUN_ID="<run-id>"
preserve_run_state || exit 1
audit_status=0
npm --silent run pipeline -- \
  --platform "$RUN_CONTROL_PLATFORM" \
  --audit "$RUN_CONTROL_RUN_ID" \
  > "$RUN_CONTROL_OBSERVATION_ROOT/audit.json" \
  2> "$RUN_CONTROL_OBSERVATION_ROOT/audit.stderr" || audit_status=$?
printf '%s\n' "$audit_status" > "$RUN_CONTROL_OBSERVATION_ROOT/audit.exit" || exit 1
test "$audit_status" -eq 0 || exit 1
```

Record the Nova run and operation IDs, Buster job ID, plan digest, source revision, and
submission time. Stop and investigate if the job identity changes for the same
operation, the state moves outside `accepted`, `running`, and a terminal state,
or Nova reports an identity or digest mismatch. A transport retry can reuse the
stored request only when its bytes and idempotency key are unchanged.

After process interruption, repeat [Inspect a Run](../operate.md#inspect-a-run)
with stopped run and adapter writers before audit or recovery. Retain original
raw bytes, require strict copied-journal inspection, and reconcile accepted
external effects through their owning contracts. Unknown outcomes or absent
reconciliation methods stop recovery. If an incident owner later authorizes
canonical tail repair, retain original bytes first and record the command and
its actual file changes. Then follow
[Recover After Interruption](../operate.md#recover-after-interruption) with the
same original project, platform, graph, package snapshot, and run identity.
Run the recovery command from the original KubeClaw checkout:

```text
npm run pipeline -- \
  --platform "<platform.json>" \
  --project "<project.json>" \
  --recover "<run-id>"
```

Recovery must use the original graph and package snapshot. It reconnects to
accepted Buster work through durable Nova state. Start a new run when governed
configuration must change. The complete core procedure and explicit-pipeline
forms are in [Operate KubeClaw](../operate.md#validate-before-starting).

## 6. Run the Local Vertical Proof

The repository includes an executable vertical proof for the protocol path.
It creates a temporary Git repository and resolves a unit-suite plan. It then
starts a real local Buster service and submits the signed source snapshot. The
proof runs the provider through Worker Core, parses JUnit, imports evidence, and
checks the Nova decision.

```text
npm run verify:test-gate:phase8
```

Run this command from the repository root after completing the linked locked
dependency installation. It creates its own
temporary repository, ports, state, source keys, and service. It does not need
a deployed Nova or Buster instance. Stop if `plugin-system:sandbox:build`
fails. Do not treat a smaller registry or resolver check as execution evidence.
The
[vertical proof source](https://github.com/datrab/kubeclaw/blob/3cf7dc4f72c2ae1e0ba4c47cceb08c98f4c70b7f/tests/verification/contracts/check-pipeline-phase8-vertical.mts)
shows the temporary project, runtime, submission, expected result, and negative
controls.

Observe the final JSON line. A valid proof has `"ok": true`, `"remote": true`,
provider `direct-command`, report `junit`, and coverage `lcov`. The command
must exit zero. Preserve the full terminal output and current Git revision as
the evidence record. An exit zero without the stated fields is not the expected
proof.

The fixture-and-matrix example is a configuration template. It proves loading,
resolution, port links, matrix expansion, and JUnit-adapter binding. It cannot
prove a live Kubernetes run until you replace its image and command placeholders
and supply the broker described in [Before You Start](#before-you-start).

> [Buster status and result are separate remote objects](https://github.com/datrab/kubeclaw/blob/3cf7dc4f72c2ae1e0ba4c47cceb08c98f4c70b7f/skills/buster/engine/test-gates/remote-plan-http.ts#L80-L178).
>
> [Nova verifies and imports each result and evidence digest](https://github.com/datrab/kubeclaw/blob/3cf7dc4f72c2ae1e0ba4c47cceb08c98f4c70b7f/skills/nova/core/test-gates/remote-result-import.ts#L156-L207).

## 7. Read The Result In The Correct Order

1. Check job identity, plan digest, source revision, and terminal state.
2. Check the gate decision and required coverage.
3. Find the first blocking node that is not passed.
4. Read every attempt, including earlier retries.
5. Separate provider `failed` assertions from `errored` execution.
6. Check fixture cleanup and retained resources.
7. Open normalized report facts, then the original report evidence when detail
   was capped or parsing failed.
8. Verify that Nova's evidence import is complete.

For a unit node, common `failed` facts are failing JUnit cases or a coverage
percentage below its minimum. Common `errored` facts are an unknown executable,
missing report, invalid XML, unsafe path, timeout, signal, output limit, or
evidence digest mismatch.

## 8. Diagnose By Boundary

| Observation | Boundary | Action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Plan never resolves | Project declaration, suite, provider schema, graph, or policy | Read the exact resolver error. Correct the declaration; do not retry transport. |
| Submission is rejected | Source/request identity, authentication, capacity, or installed registry | Compare the stored Nova job with Buster admission. Reuse the same idempotency key only for identical bytes. |
| Job remains accepted | Buster scheduler or recovery | Check readiness, durable record, concurrency, and recovered-job state. |
| Provider errors before process start | Package snapshot, grant, executable catalogue, or Worker admission | Check exact package digest, role closure, capability grant, and worker profile. |
| Process exits but node errors | Required report/evidence missing or invalid | Inspect attempt log and declared path. Do not change to exit-code mode merely to hide the report error. |
| Node is skipped | Condition or upstream outcome | Read the skip cause and coverage rule. A skip is not a pass. |
| Job completed but Nova does not decide | Result/evidence fetch, digest, receipt, or import | Preserve both stores. Repair transport or missing blob; do not rerun under the same identity with different content. |
| Cancellation appears late | Cooperative stop crossed a terminal transition | Trust the guarded terminal record. Inspect descendant cleanup before another run. |

## 9. Recover and Clean Up

For a failed local proof, keep the first error and full output. Correct the
missing host dependency, run the same command again, and compare the new Git
revision and output. The proof owns temporary directories and removes them in
its finalizer. If the process is killed, inspect only operating-system temporary
storage for a directory with the proof prefix. Do not remove project files.

For production, complete [Inspect a Run](../operate.md#inspect-a-run) before
any audit or interrupted-run recovery. Preserve verified raw run and adapter
copies with writers stopped; strict copied-journal failure preserves raw bytes
and stops the task. Do not resubmit different content with an existing job ID.
Reconnect through Nova when Buster has accepted the job. The current pipeline
CLI has no supported operator cancellation command. Process termination is not
durable cancellation. For urgent containment, preserve evidence, stop new
admission at the owning service, follow the approved incident process, and
reconcile each accepted external effect. Do not claim `cancelled` unless the
durable lifecycle record says so. See the [cancellation
boundary](../operate.md#cancellation-boundary).

Direct-command workspaces are attempt-owned and removed through Worker Core
cleanup. Fixture suites add external resources. Confirm that each fixture
cleanup is successful or that an intentional retained lease has a bounded
expiry. Retain the operation and job identities, plan and result digests,
attempt errors, evidence receipts, cleanup result, and lease expiry. Do not call
a test run complete while cleanup or retention is unknown.

## Expected Result

A successful run has one immutable plan, a committed source identity, a
terminal Buster result, passed required nodes, satisfied coverage, complete
evidence import, and proved cleanup or bounded retention. The audit path can
connect each fact to the exact provider package and attempt.

For the executable vertical proof, the command prints a JSON object with
`"ok": true`, `"remote": true`, provider `direct-command`, report `junit`, and
coverage `lcov`. A missing compiler, incompatible lock program, absent archive
tool, or denied process launch is an environment failure. It is not a passed or
failed test result.

      "owner": "Nova event journal and run state",
      "redisRole": "non-authoritative projection"

    {
      "data": "Buster job, node result, and evidence",
      "owner": "Buster durable stores",
      "redisRole": "non-authoritative transport or observation"
    },
    {
      "data": "Prism project, design request, agent job, revision, and approval",
      "owner": "Prism Control and Prism PostgreSQL",

## Choose the recovery boundary

An interrupted process is not a cancelled run. This rehearsal kills one owned
local child only after its artifact checkpoint is durable, then uses the real
Core recovery CLI with the original platform, graph and run ID. Its test stage
is intentionally a checkpoint producer/reader, not a fake implementation agent
or remote quality provider. Core, the filesystem artifact store, effect receipts,
checkpoint propagation and recovered stage attempts are real.

The successful case has no external mutation that would require a separate
continuation. Run the negative exercise too: a completed HTTP request is not
permission to repeat an interrupted external operation. A safe recovery stop is
a result to retain, not a test failure to bypass.

## Prepare the owned local exercise

Use a selected isolated checkout and the
[locked development dependencies and Node.js 24 toolchain](../../extend/developer-handbook.md#prepare-a-clean-checkout),
Git, GNU `flock`, writable private temporary storage and permission to spawn and
signal your own children. Run the following commands from the repository root.
They create and remove only their own temporary fixtures. Do not point them at
a production storage root, an operator platform or a deployed service.

```bash
node tests/verification/contracts/check-plugin-system-v2-checkpoint-recovery.mjs
node --test tests/verification/reliability/external-effect-recovery.test.mts
```

Require the first command to exit zero and print
`{"ok":true,"contract":"plugin-system-v2-checkpoint-recovery"}`. Require all
three tests in the second command to pass with no skipped case. Retain stdout,
stderr, exit statuses and the selected Source revision outside the disposable
fixtures. An early error, missing dependency, unexpected signal or failed
assertion is not an observed recovery.

## Follow the checkpoint interruption

The first command owns this exact sequence:

1. Write one platform and graph. The graph has one `test.checkpoint` stage,
   three allowed attempts, no remediation and a 60-second stage timeout. Its
   grants select the actual artifact store for `artifacts.write` and
   `artifacts.read` in namespace `test.checkpoint`.
2. Start a child with the real Core execution engine and fixed run ID
   `run:checkpoint-recovery`. The first stage attempt writes artifact
   `checkpoint:batch-1` with `checkpoint: true`, waits for its real response,
   then writes the owned readiness marker and stays in flight.
3. Wait at most 20 seconds for that marker, observing premature child exit.
   Only this marker authorizes the fixture to send `SIGKILL` to its own child.
   Wait for confirmed child exit; a submitted signal alone proves nothing.
4. Read the original lifecycle bytes after exit. Exactly one `artifact.created`
   must describe the checkpoint. No terminal run event may exist yet. This is
   an interrupted first attempt, not a completed stage or terminal run.
5. Spawn the actual Core CLI with the same platform file, graph file and
   `--recover run:checkpoint-recovery`. The engine checks its retained snapshot,
   registry/configuration identities and effect-recovery conditions. No edited
   snapshot, new run ID, changed graph or replacement artifact supplies success.
6. In attempt 2, the test stage receives the original checkpoint through
   `context.artifact`, then reads the exact namespace/ID/digest with the real
   artifact adapter. It checks the stored value before returning `passed`.
7. Require CLI exit zero, returned status `succeeded` and stage attempt number
   2. Read original lifecycle bytes again: `attempt.created` numbers are exactly
   `[1,2]`; `run.resumed` and `run.succeeded` exist; `artifact.created` still
   occurs once. Returning the earlier checkpoint does not create a second
   artifact-created event.

The script also executes a separate producer→consumer graph to check that a
declared dependent stage receives the producer's checkpoint. That is a second
run, not another attempt in the interrupted run. Its success must not hide a
failure in the first scenario.

The fixture reads its original lifecycle bytes directly and asserts the
checkpoint/attempt transition. It does not produce a retained operator incident
archive or claim that killing an arbitrary process yields a complete journal.
Its finalizer removes its private temporary tree. For a real incident, use the
next section's preservation procedure instead of treating test output as your
run's audit.

## Contrast three real external-mutation stops

The second command runs a local HTTP service that appends and fsyncs one real
mutation record. A trusted test stage invokes it through the shipped generic
runtime-dispatch, network-http and secret-resolver adapters with scoped grants.
The service is a controlled local mutation authority, not an agent completion
simulator. Its ephemeral test secret stays in the fixture environment.

- **Before receipt:** the server has durably mutated but withholds its response.
  The fixture kills the Core child. Recovery must reject with
  `RECOVERY_EFFECT_OUTCOME_UNRESOLVED`; the server mutation count stays one.
- **After receipt:** the server returns success and the stage marks receipt
  before the fixture kills the still-running child. Recovery must reject with
  `RECOVERY_EXTERNAL_CONTINUATION_REQUIRED`; a successful receipt cannot supply
  the interrupted plugin's missing continuation.
- **Lost response:** the server mutates then closes the connection. Core returns
  `blocked` after one stage attempt, despite a three-attempt ceiling. Recovery
  rejects the terminal run with `RECOVERY_RUN_TERMINAL`; the mutation count
  still stays one.

Each case requires exactly one original mutation line. No test clears a durable
request or manufactures a terminal receipt so the operation can run again.
These are explicit recovery stops, not evidence of a general reconciliation
CLI. Core permits local artifact checkpoint recovery and repeated reads; its
safe-operation list does not include arbitrary external mutations.

## Apply the procedure to an owned real run

Use [Inspect a Run](../operate.md#inspect-a-run) before audit or recovery. Confirm
that the run owner exited, stop original run and owning-adapter writers, retain
complete raw copies and manifests, and strictly parse each copied journal.
Opening audit/recovery can create locks or truncate an incomplete tail; never
use it to make an uninspected original pass. Unknown writer ownership, a
partial/corrupt chain or an unexplained external outcome stops the task.

Keep the original platform, pipeline/project, package/configuration snapshot,
storage root and run ID. Follow the exact explicit-graph/project command in
[Recover After Interruption](../operate.md#recover-after-interruption), not a
new start command. Observe the actual returned status and exit code. A wait
needs its matching signal, a cooldown needs its recorded time, and a missing
receipt/continuation needs the owning authority; increasing attempt budgets
cannot waive these checks.

After the recovery process exits, repeat stopped-writer raw preservation and
strict inspection before the final audit. Compare original identities, journal
heads, attempts, checkpoint artifact producer/digest and external receipts.
Claim successful recovery only when the returned terminal state and final audit
agree without unexplained duplicated effects. Otherwise retain the exact stop
and owning follow-up. Do not recover a terminal run or edit its journal.

Cleanup belongs to the original run and adapter owners. The local test's
finalizer has no authority over a deployed run, external resource, credential or
artifact retention policy. Preserve the initial failure and all recovery
attempts; removing evidence is not a recovery action.

## Choose fixture storage

Use a persistent volume claim (PVC) only when the fixture needs persistent data.
Before resolving the run, compare each claim in the checked manifest with the
configured fixture runtime's storage policy. Ask the platform owner to confirm
the selected StorageClass, provisioner and reclaim policy. Stop if the selected
class or its data-retention behavior is unknown.

- Select an explicit, nonempty `storageClassName` from `allowedStorageClasses`.
  Omit that field only when `allowDefaultStorageClass` permits the cluster's
  default class. An empty string is not the omitted-field route.
- Set `resources.requests.storage` to a positive whole-byte quantity within
  `maximumClaimBytes`. Keep the combined requested size within `maximumTotalBytes`.
  A standalone PVC counts once. Each StatefulSet claim template counts once per
  declared replica; omitted replicas count as one.
- Use filesystem volumes. An omitted `volumeMode` is permitted; an explicit
  value must be `Filesystem`. The runtime rejects `volumeName`, `selector`,
  `dataSource` and `dataSourceRef`, so this route cannot select an existing
  volume, clone a claim or restore a snapshot through those fields.
- Leave `metadata.namespace` out of the checked manifest. The fixture assigns
  its controlled namespace; an explicit namespace is rejected.

[Claim selection and replica counting](https://github.com/datrab/kubeclaw/blob/28e4f1b6a2e736dc936b48847cf422dcc0a25da2/skills/buster/engine/test-gates/kubernetes-fixture-runtime.ts#L202-L222),
[per-claim policy checks](https://github.com/datrab/kubeclaw/blob/28e4f1b6a2e736dc936b48847cf422dcc0a25da2/skills/buster/engine/test-gates/kubernetes-fixture-runtime.ts#L232-L254)
and [namespace and total-size checks](https://github.com/datrab/kubeclaw/blob/28e4f1b6a2e736dc936b48847cf422dcc0a25da2/skills/buster/engine/test-gates/kubernetes-fixture-runtime.ts#L315-L330)
define these KubeClaw restrictions. See the
[runtime configuration reference](../../reference/buster-runtime-configuration.md)
for their configuration authority.

A passed manifest check proves that these requests meet the runtime policy. It
does not prove volume provisioning, binding, mounting or deletion on the target
cluster. During the run, retain the actual claim and volume identities, binding
state and workload observations. Before cleanup, confirm which data may be lost
and who owns any retained backing volume. If cleanup is uncertain, inspect those
same resources before retrying; do not infer data removal from lease deletion.
The controller's
[retention and cleanup boundary](../../understand/buster-namespace-controller.md#retention-decisions-and-cleanup)
explains which namespace deletion effects remain separate from storage policy.

## Prepare, observe and release

1. Follow the [Buster suite workflow](buster-suite.md#before-you-start)
   for the checked-out version, execution host, installed tools and platform
   binding. Its maintained example requires your real image and manifest-check
   command; its placeholders do not establish a runnable deployment.
2. Select one digest-pinned image, either through the `image` input or through
   fixture configuration. Supply one `checked-manifest` artifact with the
   declared media type, digest and file location. The provider rejects an image
   supplied by both routes. The runtime checks the manifest bytes and permitted
   workload, Service and storage facts before it requests the lease.
   [Provider input checks](https://github.com/datrab/kubeclaw/blob/28e4f1b6a2e736dc936b48847cf422dcc0a25da2/skills/buster/plugins/kubernetes-fixture/src/provider.js#L18-L35)
   and [runtime manifest checks](https://github.com/datrab/kubeclaw/blob/28e4f1b6a2e736dc936b48847cf422dcc0a25da2/skills/buster/engine/test-gates/kubernetes-fixture-runtime.ts#L650-L677)
   define these boundaries.
3. Resolve the plan before starting it, using the workflow's
   [resolution procedure](buster-suite.md#4-resolve-before-you-run).
   Check the selected fixture, linked artifact, namespace prefix, service ports,
   retention and capability grant. Stop on a resolver or policy rejection.
4. Use the workflow's [submit and observe procedure](buster-suite.md#5-submit-and-observe-in-production).
   Preserve the run, node and attempt identities. Successful preparation returns
   the `deployment` output with lease name, namespace, image and manifest digest,
   creation time, expiry and endpoint. Dedicated generated credentials, when
   requested, use a separate `demo-credentials` output. A returned endpoint is
   not evidence that a later network request succeeded.
   [Output construction](https://github.com/datrab/kubeclaw/blob/28e4f1b6a2e736dc936b48847cf422dcc0a25da2/skills/buster/plugins/kubernetes-fixture/src/provider.js#L115-L128)
   defines the observations to retain.
   The basic lease wait checks phase `Ready` or `Rejected`; it does not compare
   the lease UID or generation. Read
   [each controller observation at its own level](../../understand/buster-namespace-controller.md#read-each-observation-at-its-own-level)
   when verifying ownership or dedicated credential provenance.
   [The basic wait loop](https://github.com/datrab/kubeclaw/blob/28e4f1b6a2e736dc936b48847cf422dcc0a25da2/skills/buster/engine/test-gates/kubernetes-fixture-runtime.ts#L525-L540)
   is narrower than those proofs.
5. Inspect cleanup through the same run's result and audit. With retention mode
   `delete`, provider cleanup invokes release and requires `ok: true`. With
   `retain`, that cleanup method returns without requesting release; the lease's
   expiry and controller retention policy still bound its lifetime. Keep the
   lease identity and expiry when investigating retained resources. Namespace
   deletion does not prove that a backing volume was erased; its reclaim policy
   remains a separate storage boundary. Use the
   [retention and cleanup explanation](../../understand/buster-namespace-controller.md#retention-decisions-and-cleanup)
   before removing a lease or workload.

If apply returns an error, preparation has not entered its protected cleanup
block. The write result can be uncertain. Inspect the exact lease identity before
another attempt. If a later preparation step fails, its cleanup attempt can also
fail while the original preparation error is reported. Explicit release instead
propagates its deletion failure. Preserve the first error, run identities,
returned fixture details and cleanup result; use the
[failure and recovery guide](../../understand/buster-namespace-controller.md#diagnose-failures-and-resume-safely)
to establish retained state. A new attempt derives a new fixture identity and
does not prove that an earlier fixture was removed.
[Identity derivation](https://github.com/datrab/kubeclaw/blob/28e4f1b6a2e736dc936b48847cf422dcc0a25da2/skills/buster/plugins/kubernetes-fixture/src/provider.js#L80-L84)
and [the apply and cleanup boundary](https://github.com/datrab/kubeclaw/blob/28e4f1b6a2e736dc936b48847cf422dcc0a25da2/skills/buster/engine/test-gates/kubernetes-fixture-runtime.ts#L709-L744)
are the source authorities. These procedures require target-cluster observations;
local package checks establish only their declared boundaries.

## Goal and boundary

Start in a selected checkout, materialize real platform and graph inputs, validate
the installed registry and grants, run a shipped stage through the real Core CLI,
preserve durable state, audit both outcomes, verify an original artifact's bytes
and producing attempt, correlate same-run observer deliveries and durable local
telemetry, and clean up only the owned fixture.

The stage is `kubeclaw.lint.delivery`. It reads a real disposable repository
Dockerfile through `kubeclaw.repository-adapter:repository` and writes its report
through `kubeclaw.artifact-store:artifact-store`. Core owns the actual snapshots,
event/effect journals, attempts, terminal states and adapter shutdown. No fake
runner, hand-built lifecycle event, memory journal, model or provider result is
used.

This is **one local explicit-graph workflow**, not the eight-stage
`nova-project.v2` implementation project. It validates and normalizes the graph
through the actual Core preparation path; it does not run the Nova project
compiler. The [first-project exercise](README.md#materialize-and-compile-a-first-project)
owns that separate compile-only task. This journey does not execute Forge,
remote Buster, an image build, a test provider, a cluster, Redis, a deployed
telemetry collector, demo delivery or human acceptance. It uses one shipped
local telemetry observer and file sink for the same two explicit-graph runs. A local artifact report is not an
application delivery result.

## Prepare a checkout and host

Use a new isolated checkout that includes this maintained guide/helper at the
selected revision. Never install dependencies into another active shared
checkout. Clone and prepare through the
[developer handbook](../../extend/developer-handbook.md#prepare-a-clean-checkout),
using its locked Node.js 24 development-dependency installation and owned writable
npm cache. Keep its selected full source revision; do not substitute a random
current branch while comparing results.

From that repository root, check:

```bash
set -euo pipefail
export CORE_SOURCE_REVISION="$(git rev-parse HEAD)"
git cat-file -e "$CORE_SOURCE_REVISION:docs/site/use/workflows/examples/local-core.mjs"
test -z "$(git status --porcelain)"
node --version
git --version
/usr/bin/flock --version
node -e 'for (const name of ["typescript", "ajv", "ajv-formats"]) console.log(require.resolve(name))'
```

Node must be major 24. `/usr/bin/flock` must be GNU util-linux with `--timeout`;
a BusyBox command or a different executable on PATH does not satisfy the
absolute-path lock contract. Use a local filesystem qualified for the required
locks, append writes and fsync. A generic network mount is not qualified by
this exercise.

The caller needs permission to create a private disposable directory, initialize
and commit a local Git repository with an example-only identity, read the shipped
package roots, start Node child processes and write private fixture stores. No
network or production credential, cluster context, Docker, browser, external
model, Go compiler or service is needed by this selected graph. Its builtin
packages run through the existing trusted in-process path; this is not a native
sandbox/cgroup isolation test.

Stop on a missing dependency/tool, wrong source revision or dirty selected
checkout. Correct preparation rather than removing a grant or weakening schema
validation. The source revision recorded in the fixture identifies the checkout;
actual registry content digests separately identify the installed package bytes.

## 1. Materialize the complete inputs

Keep the same Bash shell through all steps. The final component below must not
exist. The parent temporary directory is newly allocated by this shell.

```bash
export LOCAL_CORE_PARENT="$(mktemp -d /tmp/kubeclaw-local-core.XXXXXX)"
export LOCAL_CORE="$LOCAL_CORE_PARENT/journey"
node docs/site/use/workflows/examples/local-core.mjs prepare "$LOCAL_CORE"
```

Expected JSON: `status: "prepared"`, `execution: false`, the selected source
revision, and your exact destination. Keep both paths. A failed preparation can
leave a partial private tree; do not run into it again or erase an unknown path.
Retain its first error, correct the prerequisite and select a different new
parent/destination.

Inspect the materialized inputs before starting:

```bash
cat "$LOCAL_CORE/platform.json"
cat "$LOCAL_CORE/success.pipeline.json"
cat "$LOCAL_CORE/blocked.pipeline.json"
cat "$LOCAL_CORE/denied-platform.json"
cat "$LOCAL_CORE/source.json"
```

The helper creates:

- A committed disposable repository with `Dockerfile`, one static file and a
  literal `COPY site/ /srv/site/` declaration. No image is built.
- A complete `pipeline-platform.v2`: the shipped Nova/common package installation
  roots and builtin trust roots, one fixed repository adapter, an artifact store,
  exact provider selections and narrow stage grants. The registry discovers all
  current packages in those roots; it activates only the selected one stage and
  three adapters and one telemetry observer. Registry package count is not a
  supported fixed constant.
- A complete one-stage `pipeline-definition.v2` with concurrency one, one attempt,
  zero technical retries/repair cycles and a 10-second stage deadline. The
  successful input binds `moduleId: site`, `Dockerfile` and `/srv/site/`.
- A separately granted `kubeclaw.telemetry-observer:telemetry`, with empty
  config and event-prefix grants derived from its actual registered subscriptions,
  bound to `kubeclaw.telemetry-store:telemetry`. Its private `telemetry/` store
  allows 64 KiB records, 256 records and 4 MiB total; it has no network or Secret.
- A second graph whose Dockerfile path contains `../`; the stage must block it
  before repository read, while persisting a diagnostic report.
- A second platform with the stage's artifact-write grant missing; registry/grant
  validation must reject it before execution.
- A private ownership marker used for safe fixture cleanup. It is not a product
  authorization token.

`platform.json` selects `artifacts.write` only for namespace
`kubeclaw.delivery-lint` and `git.repository.read` only for `Dockerfile`.
Adapter configuration fixes the disposable repository and its exact Git HEAD.
The artifact budget is 64 KiB per blob with 100 metadata records and 1 MiB total
configured store capacity. The helper generates no credential or secret value.

## 2. Validate and execute the actual product

```bash
node docs/site/use/workflows/examples/local-core.mjs run "$LOCAL_CORE"
```

This command is a maintained orchestration helper, not a replacement engine.
Read [its complete source](examples/local-core.mjs). In order it:

1. Uses the real platform/graph loaders and `validatePipelineRuntimeV2` to check
   schema, installed packages, selected stage/adapters, configuration and grants.
2. Checks that the missing artifact grant causes a relevant admission failure.
3. Invokes the actual Core CLI with `success.pipeline.json`, the original
   `platform.json`, and `run:local-core-success`.
4. Invokes that CLI with `blocked.pipeline.json` and the separate
   `run:local-core-blocked` identity, expecting exit one and durable `blocked`.
5. Waits for each synchronous child to exit after the real engine awaits its
   final serialized observer drain and adapter shutdown. This private fixture has no other authorized writer.
6. Copies the complete run, artifact and telemetry trees to `raw-before-audit`,
   records their exact byte digests, and strictly parses copied event/effect,
   observer-delivery and checkpoint journals before invoking audit on canonical
   state. It also validates the copied telemetry record store with the original
   pure replay validator; it does not open the copy as a writable store. Audit can open/repair a journal;
   retained raw bytes come first. A parse failure stops before audit.
7. Uses the same original CLI platform and run IDs to audit each run, verifies
   audit/head/terminal correlation, reconstructs successful state through the
   original read-only evidence reader, verifies its artifact blob, and checks
   every selected canonical event against its observer delivery, checkpoint,
   telemetry effect and durable sink record.

Every CLI invocation, actual exit status, stdout and stderr is retained in
`*.command.json`, `*.stdout` and `*.stderr`. No failed command is changed to a
passing receipt. The two audit invocations are actual `--audit` operations, not
synthetic event summaries. Do not remove the helper's fixed assertions to force
an unrelated installation through this fixture.

## 3. Inspect the observations and artifact

Expected final JSON includes:

- `status: "verified-local-core-journey"`;
- success run `succeeded` and negative run `blocked`;
- `blockedReason: "delivery_lint.path_invalid"`;
- `missingGrant: "rejected-before-execution"`;
- an exact `delivery-lint:site` artifact reference in namespace
  `kubeclaw.delivery-lint`, digest, byte size and producing run/stage/attempt;
- the actual journal head, event count and effect head;
- `telemetry` identifying the shipped observer/provider, stream
  `telemetry/plugin-events`, actual record count, both run IDs, each terminal
  checkpoint and zero delivery failures; and
- `rawBytesPreserved: true` plus the explicit local-only execution scope.

Do not hardcode attempt UUIDs or journal/effect digests. They identify this run's
actual bytes and timestamps, not universal example constants.

```bash
cat "$LOCAL_CORE/validation.json"
cat "$LOCAL_CORE/denied-admission.json"
cat "$LOCAL_CORE/success-run.stdout"
cat "$LOCAL_CORE/blocked-run.stdout"
cat "$LOCAL_CORE/success-audit.stdout"
cat "$LOCAL_CORE/blocked-audit.stdout"
cat "$LOCAL_CORE/verification.json"
node docs/site/use/workflows/examples/local-core.mjs verify "$LOCAL_CORE"
```

The verification command rereads retained bytes; it does not rerun a stage or
repair a journal. It requires exact raw-tree equality, strict hash-linked journal
parsing, actual audit digest/head/event agreement and the same producing attempt.
It reads the original durable artifact blob by its recorded digest, checks byte
count and SHA-256, parses the report and requires `passed: true` with no failures.
The successful result is a Delivery Lint report, not a provider's test result or
a signed product-acceptance attestation.

The invalid-path run must have a blocked stage result and no repository-read
effect. Its diagnostic artifact write is expected: blocked does not mean
“nothing was persisted.” The missing-grant branch is a separate admission
rejection, not the same error and not a passing negative run.

## Same-run telemetry and its authority

The file sink is a projection, not a second canonical lifecycle journal. The
helper discovers the enabled observer and its subscriptions/provenance from
each original run snapshot, then selects that run's subscribed canonical
events. It requires exactly one sink record for each selected event, no
extra/unowned records, and this complete correlation:

1. Canonical event ID, sequence, run and terminal type come from the strictly
   parsed preserved event journal, not from an expected event list.
2. Observer delivery history must contain exactly started then completed at
   attempt one for every selected event, with the same observer/event/run and
   no error. Checkpoints must advance to each event under the snapshot's exact
   observer provenance, including the terminal run event.
3. The same run's effect journal must contain its telemetry request, acceptance
   and completed receipt under stable `delivery:<observer>:<event>:1` identity.
   The request must carry the original observer envelope; the receipt must
   identify the actual persisted sink sequence and accepted append.
4. The copied store must pass the product's pure durable-record replay/digest/
   sequence checks. Every record belongs to that run and stream. Its content
   must equal the original product telemetry envelope after the original sink
   projection/redaction, not a hand-built success observation.

The observer subscribes to its manifest's event set; this graph does not emit
all supported lifecycle types. The engine serializes drain callbacks and awaits
one final drain before adapter shutdown. The sink awaits its durable append
before acknowledging it. Waiting for the real child to exit gives this private
fixture its stopped-writer preservation boundary; it is not proof that every
third-party observer honors shutdown.

The shipped observer uses best-effort policy. A successful stage/CLI status
alone therefore cannot prove telemetry delivery. This helper separately rejects
missing, duplicate, failed or incomplete deliveries, absent terminal checkpoint,
missing effect receipt, wrong owner/provenance, or changed telemetry bytes. It
never turns a best-effort failure into a stronger pipeline lifecycle state.
Read `verification.json` for this execution's actual record/event counts and
identities; do not copy attempt UUIDs or digest values into another run.

This local check establishes same-run stored telemetry alongside audit and
artifact evidence. It does not establish Redis delivery, a remote dashboard,
all observer failure/replay scenarios, production redaction of arbitrary text,
or deployed collection. Keep lifecycle authority, observer acknowledgement and
sink retention separate; see [Telemetry](../../understand/telemetry.md).

## Failure, recovery and stop decisions

| Observation | Meaning and safe action |
| --- | --- |
| Destination already exists or ownership/revision differs | Stop. Keep the partial fixture and error; choose a new private destination after correcting preparation. |
| Tool/import/lock error | Host prerequisite failure, not a pipeline verdict. Prepare the same supported toolchain; never replace durable journals with memory journals. |
| Stage owner/config/grant validation fails unexpectedly | Inspect the selected installed roots, package versions and exact grants. Do not broaden authority or call a missing stage successful. |
| Expected-success CLI exits nonzero | Retain actual stdout/stderr and original run bytes. Stop; do not change the graph and recover the same run ID. |
| Negative path succeeds, reads the repository, or lacks its blocked reason | Failed safety expectation. Preserve evidence and investigate the owning stage/runtime before any claim of completion. |
| Child response is lost, timeout occurs or writers might remain active | Stop. Establish actual owner exit and stopped adapter writers through the normal [run-control procedure](../operate.md#inspect-a-run) before preservation/audit. A helper timeout is not durable cancellation. |
| Raw copy, strict parse, audit, artifact hash or telemetry correlation check fails | Preserve the original files and first error. Do not repair/rewrite/remove them to make a comparison pass. Follow [recovery](../recovery.md) under the owning store authority. |
| CLI succeeded but observer delivery/checkpoint/effect/sink evidence is missing or failed | Local telemetry task has not completed. Preserve both stores and journals; inspect the selected observer/provider/grants and store limits. Do not rerun a terminal run to manufacture evidence or claim that best-effort delivery changed lifecycle. |
| Run is already terminal | Inspect retained evidence. Do not recover or repeat the same run ID; prepare a new disposable journey if new execution is intended. |

The helper has no retry/resume/repair implementation. That is deliberate:
this graph has no wait or repair edge. Use the separately maintained
[wait/resume](wait-resume.md) guide for that task, with its actual authority and
execution limits. Do not infer those outcomes from this success.

## Cleanup and remaining data

First retain any results needed outside the private fixture: selected source
revision, input JSON, command/exit output, final verification and actual audit,
raw run/artifact/telemetry copies and their manifest, observer delivery and
checkpoint histories, and the matching telemetry effect receipts. These local example records contain
no production credential, but remain under your normal retention decisions.
No running process or external resource should remain after successful verify.

Then remove only the marker-bound, fully verified fixture and its now-empty
new parent:

```bash
node docs/site/use/workflows/examples/local-core.mjs cleanup "$LOCAL_CORE"
rmdir -- "$LOCAL_CORE_PARENT"
```

Expected JSON is `status: "owned-fixture-removed"` with your exact root and both
run IDs. Cleanup first repeats verification and refuses absent/changed ownership,
missing verification or changed raw evidence. It does not delete the source
checkout, dependency cache, another storage root or any external object.
`rmdir` fails instead of deleting an unexpected nonempty parent. If verification
failed, this cleanup command intentionally refuses: preserve the partial tree
and diagnose it rather than inventing successful cleanup.

## Before an owned outage exercise

Use one explicitly selected Nova run/event and the exact activated observer,
package snapshot, provider, target, Redis database/endpoint and stream prefix.
Record these separately from the role-health stream. Capture the original event
ID, sequence, run identity, observer delivery ID, last valid checkpoint,
started/completed/failed delivery attempts and corresponding effect request and
receipt. Use [Inspect a Run](../operate.md#inspect-a-run) with run/adapter writers
stopped and raw copies strictly parsed before audit. Preserve the Redis store
and retention/dedup settings under its owner too.

The actual transport stream is:

`<streamPrefix>:v2:<publisher|telemetry>:<encodeURIComponent(target)>`

The kind matters: the transport-publisher and telemetry registrations do not
share a stream. A period and underscore in target names remain distinct. The
dedup key appends `:dedup:` and SHA-256 of the canonical JSON idempotency-key
string. Use the returned receipt's exact `stream` and `entryId`, not a hand
sanitization of the target or the latest entry in a similarly named stream.

The operator must establish its authorized read path to that exact Redis
stream and, when applicable, consumer group. This package writes streams; it
does not create/own a consumer group or acknowledge an external consumer's work.
A deployment-specific consumer's `XACK` is not Core delivery completion. If no
consumer exists, record “no configured consumer”, not an invented consumer
baseline or a zero backlog claim.

## Legacy namespace cutover

Do not treat an upgrade from legacy underscore-sanitized stream names as a
normal v2 reconnect. The old mapping is not reversible: dots and underscores
could collapse into the same target name. Upgrade actual writers and consumers
together. Pause legacy writers, reconcile pending deliveries under their
original event/receipt identities and inspect retained legacy records before
switching consumers to the exact v2 names. If the external consumer inventory
or pending-delivery reconciliation is unavailable, retain that migration stop;
a healthy new stream does not establish completion.

The package does not rename, copy, republish, trim or delete old streams, migrate
external consumers, or change the configured `MAXLEN` and dedup TTL policy.
There is no supplied automatic migration command or consumer-group lookup.
The separate OpenClaw host-observer Redis transport is unaffected by this Nova
plugin cutover. Preserve old records under their owners rather than inventing
new canonical events or manually filling the new stream.

[The package's explicit upgrade boundary](https://github.com/datrab/kubeclaw/blob/ce7740252864a9b547bee8a35260d6ab10c9f05e/skills/common/plugins/redis-transport/README.md#L16-L24)
is Source guidance, not evidence that a deployed migration has run.

## Judge restoration and backlog separately

After the approved fault, restore the exact recorded Redis configuration,
replica/PVC identity and credentials using the owning procedure. A healthy role
only permits the delivery investigation to continue. Compare original Nova raw
event bytes and journal head before/during/after; retain any difference rather
than attributing it to Redis automatically.

Then classify the selected event from its original observer history:

- **Checkpoint already covers the event:** runtime skips it. No new observer
  callback or stream append should follow from a normal repeated drain.
- **Delivery completed but checkpoint was not retained:** runtime rebuilds its
  completed-delivery set, commits the derived checkpoint without invoking the
  callback again, and preserves the existing delivery records. Do not delete a
  production checkpoint to recreate the test or turn this internal rebuild
  into permission for arbitrary checkpoint repair.
- **Delivery still has retry allowance:** an owning runtime's drain applies the
  persisted attempt count and declared policy, not a new counter after restart.
  Normal observer effect keys remain stable across delivery retries. Inspect
  original effect receipts and the sink acknowledgement; an already-recorded
  failure or uncertain external outcome does not automatically become another
  successful network attempt because Redis is healthy.
- **Attempts exhausted:** `OBSERVER_DELIVERY_ATTEMPTS_EXHAUSTED` remains exhausted
  after reconstruction. Redis restoration does not reset the budget. The
  canonical event and failed delivery history remain. With `best_effort`, later
  events for that observer/run stop during that drain; other observers/runs can
  continue. With `required`, runtime throws
  `REQUIRED_OBSERVER_DELIVERY_FAILED` and aborts the drain instead.
- **Checkpoint provenance/sequence/event or delivery transition conflicts:**
  stop. Restore/investigate the original compatible bytes and package snapshot;
  do not choose a checkpoint by timestamp or delete failed attempts.

The repository exposes no generic operator CLI to rewind an observer checkpoint,
reset exhausted delivery attempts or clear an effect receipt and replay a
terminal run. Core `--recover` rejects terminal runs; starting a new run is not
replay. If normal owned delivery cannot continue under its original contract,
retain the exact event/delivery/receipt and safe stop. The Nova observer owner
and selected adapter/Redis owner must define an authorized original-identity
continuation; absence of that supported operation is not permission to edit
journals or send a raw Redis `XADD`.

## Verify deduplication without claiming exactly-once delivery

Redis's adapter atomically checks its dedup key, appends with `XADD MAXLEN ~`
only when absent, then stores the resulting entry ID with its configured TTL.
An identical repeated key returns that original entry ID while the dedup key
survives. The script does not compare repeated payload bytes; Core's effect
identity/payload checks are a separate protection. Do not deliberately change
payload under an old key.

Dedup TTL expiry, Redis data loss or a changed prefix/kind/target/key can permit
a new entry. Approximate stream trimming can also remove an old entry while a
dedup key still returns its ID. Therefore a matching receipt is not proof that
the entry remains readable, and a restarted stream is not an exactly-once
consumer guarantee. Verify the exact original payload/identity through the
sink and consumer authority; retain uncertainty when retention prevents it.

For an isolated local **native Redis** contract check, use a selected checkout,
Node.js 24, GNU `flock`, locked dependencies and a real `redis-server` with its
sibling `redis-cli`. The fixture owns its loopback port, temporary server/data,
password and finalizer; do not supply a deployed Redis endpoint or credential.

```bash
export REDIS_SERVER="<absolute-path-to-real-redis-server>"
test -x "$REDIS_SERVER"
test -x "$(dirname "$REDIS_SERVER")/redis-cli"
node --test tests/verification/reliability/redis-transport.test.mts
```

Require all three tests to pass without skipping the native case. The native
case sends the same delivery key through the actual adapter/real Redis for
publisher and telemetry kinds with two distinct targets. It verifies four
separate exact streams and one original entry in each. Same-journal replay
reuses the effect receipt; a fresh **test-only** effect journal forces a second
physical send so actual Lua dedup must return the same original entry ID.
Creating fresh production journals to force retransmission is not a supported
operator procedure. This check demonstrates bounded per-stream dedup, not a
controlled observer outage or external consumer recovery.

The accompanying original socket tests check bounded RESP framing, fragmented
UTF-8 and prompt rejection/closure of malformed responses. The package's
`live-function` test uses a local RESP-speaking TCP fixture, not native Redis;
do not substitute its green result for this command's native-server proof.

## Reproduce observer-history controls separately

```bash
node --test tests/verification/reliability/observer-recovery.test.mts
```

This fixture installs a local file-writing observer, causes an actual missing
sink-directory error and exhausts two attempts. Reconstructing after creating
the directory must still report exhaustion without writing the old event.
A separate run/event then succeeds. Removing only that fixture's derived
checkpoint tests reconstruction from completed delivery history without a
second sink write, followed by a no-op drain. These are real file-journal and
observer behaviors, **not Redis delivery** and not permission to remove an
operator checkpoint. Keep those proof scopes separate.

## Cleanup and completion

For the deployed fault, retain original consumer/target/PVC identities, restored
replica count, exact stream/entry observations, event/checkpoint/delivery/effect
history, failed attempts and the final continuation or stop decision. Remove
only owned fault controls after restoration checks; do not purge streams,
failed journals, credentials or canonical event state to hide a gap. Redis and
consumer retention belong to their separate owners.

A complete same-run no-duplicate recovery observation requires the original
selected event to retain its identity, an allowed owner continuation, a matching
final delivery/checkpoint and exactly the intended sink/consumer observation.
Where the supported continuation is unavailable or the dedup/retention window
expired, report that exact limit. Native adapter dedup and role-health recovery
alone do not establish this stronger outcome.

## What this rehearsal changes

Run an intentionally failing **test checker** through the actual Core CLI,
retain its original event/effect journals and artifact store, then distinguish
technical retry from a source repair and the check that follows it. This is not
a full Nova implementation project or a live Forge, review-agent or Buster
provider verdict. No mocked Core runner or prewritten lifecycle record supplies
the result.

The repository's `test.repair-budget:execute` fixture has two modes. `source`
changes a private repository's `version.txt` and commits the change with real
Git. `check` reads that version and emits a deterministic finding selected by
its input. Both write real evidence through the shipped artifact store. These
are deliberately trusted in-process test stages: their direct Git/filesystem
access is not an example of capability-mediated production plugin isolation.
Never substitute a real project path or trust an external package to recreate
this rehearsal.

The [local shipped-stage workflow](local-core.md) owns the separate actual
Delivery Lint, repository-adapter, artifact and telemetry example. A test
checker's `passed` result here does not prove that an application passed a
production lint, review or test gate.

## Prepare and run

Prepare Node.js 24, Git, Linux GNU `flock` and the locked development/runtime
dependencies through the [developer handbook](../../extend/developer-handbook.md#prepare-a-clean-checkout).
Use an isolated selected checkout and run from its repository root. The helper
copies the existing test package and production artifact store into each
private fixture, links that checkout's dependency directory and trusts only
those copied roots. It needs no network, agent credential, Redis or cluster.
Keep the selected checkout and dependency bytes unchanged until cleanup.

```bash
export REPAIR_REHEARSAL="$(mktemp -d)/repair-rehearsal"
node docs/site/use/workflows/examples/repair-retry.mjs prepare "$REPAIR_REHEARSAL"
node docs/site/use/workflows/examples/repair-retry.mjs run "$REPAIR_REHEARSAL"
```

`prepare` must return `status: prepared`, `execution: false` and the actual
selected Source revision. `run` must return
`status: verified-core-retry-repair-rehearsal`. Do not equate CLI exit 1 with an
unexpected harness failure: the helper expects it for the deliberately blocked
and waiting Core outcomes and separately validates their JSON status. Missing
imports, an unexpected process exit, invalid journals or failed assertions are
errors; preserve the entire fixture and stop. An exclusive `run-started.json` intent precedes every Core child and remains
after error or interruption. Even an intent with no command result blocks
another `run`; do not delete it to retry. A partial run is not resumable by
rerunning `run`; use `verify` only for completed observations or prepare a new
fixture after diagnosing the failure.

### The frozen graph and budgets

Each scenario has its own real platform and graph files. Read them before using
the pattern elsewhere:

```bash
cat "$REPAIR_REHEARSAL/mixed/platform.json"
cat "$REPAIR_REHEARSAL/mixed/pipeline.json"
```

The ordinary chain is `source → lint → review → test`. Each check declares
`on.request_fix: source` and its own repair category. The source owns two
automatic orders per category and at most one additional orchestrator-authorized
order. Every stage explicitly declares nine maximum attempts, seven remediation
cycles, one technical retry and a 5,000 ms timeout. These are this fixture's
values, not inherited defaults or the project compiler's exact budget.

A retry repeats the same stage without spending a repair order. A trusted
`request_fix` result spends the requesting category's allowance and follows the
frozen repair edge. Core retains that finding, invalidates affected downstream
results and schedules the source stage. The successful source attempt produces
a new revision; checks must evaluate that revision rather than reuse old facts.

## Read the three outcomes

### 1. Retry, repair and recheck succeed

`mixed` requests one technical retry on source attempt 1. That attempt does not
change the repository. The next source attempt commits version 1. The lint
checker requests a repair at version 1, review at version 2 and test at version
3. Source repairs create versions 2, 3 and 4 respectively. Every invalidated
check runs again; its attempt count is not another category debit.

Expected final status is `succeeded`. Source has five attempts, one technical
retry and exactly three ledger orders, in category order `lint`, `review`,
`test`. Lint has four attempts, review three and test two. The initial source
attempt and technical retry are not repair orders. The final original journal
contains 132 events for this selected fixture and implementation; use identities,
results and the ledger, not event count alone, to decide what occurred.

### 2. Technical allowance ends without a repair order

`technical-exhausted` returns `retry` for both source attempts. Core spends its
one technical retry, then blocks. Expected source attempts: two; technical
retries: one; repair ledger: empty; final status: `blocked` (21 events in the
verified fixture). Increasing a category allowance would not restore technical
retry authority. Do not edit an existing graph or start a new run to disguise
the exhausted original attempt.

### 3. One exact extra order cannot authorize unlimited work

`extra-order` requests lint repairs at source versions 1, 2 and 3. Two automatic
lint orders produce versions 2 and 3. The next request exhausts that category
and creates an orchestrator wait. Read the preserved original wait in
`run.stdout`; it binds the exact request/history digest, wait and issuer.

The helper first submits the same signal envelope with a wrong pending digest.
Expect `REPAIR_AUTHORIZATION_INVALID`; original lifecycle event bytes must remain
identical. It then submits one valid `resume-signal.v2` with the actual wait,
signal type and issuer, the current pending digest and an explicit reason.
This local fixture acts as its configured test orchestrator; copying its issuer
text is not production identity authentication.

The accepted signal authorizes one source repair directly; it does not rerun the
known-failing lint check before repair. Source reaches version 4, and lint's
recheck passes. The test checker then requests another repair. Core blocks even
though that category had unused automatic allowance: after an extra order,
later repair needs operator action, not an automatic category reset.

Expected final status is `blocked`, source attempts four, ledger categories
`lint, lint, lint`, exactly one authorized ledger entry, lint attempts four, and
the test's pending repair category `test` (98 final events in the verified
fixture). A real administrator must use the supported separate authority path
or retain the stop; the helper neither fabricates another signal nor modifies
the journal.

## Audit original findings and replay

Each Core CLI child exits before the helper copies the **complete** scenario
`state/` and `artifacts/` trees. It records their byte manifest and strictly
parses every copied run journal before invoking the real audit CLI. Thus an
audit's journal-open behavior cannot replace the pre-audit raw bytes.
`extra-order` also retains a fresh capture immediately before the rejected
signal, before valid resume and before the final audit. `verify` checks the
manifest and strictly parses every copied run journal in each capture. All writers belong to those completed child processes; this
private-fixture fact does not establish a writer fence for a deployed system.

Inspect the retained command status and original audit rather than inferring
success from a terminal shell alone:

```bash
cat "$REPAIR_REHEARSAL/mixed/run.command.json"
cat "$REPAIR_REHEARSAL/mixed/run.stdout"
cat "$REPAIR_REHEARSAL/mixed/first-audit.stdout"
cat "$REPAIR_REHEARSAL/extra-order/invalid-resume.stderr"
cat "$REPAIR_REHEARSAL/extra-order/resume.stdout"
cat "$REPAIR_REHEARSAL/extra-order/final-audit.stdout"
node docs/site/use/workflows/examples/repair-retry.mjs verify "$REPAIR_REHEARSAL"
```

`verify` recomputes retained raw-tree hashes, strictly parses the original
preserved event chain and folds it through the real lifecycle recovery reducer.
Every reconstructed stage state must equal the final CLI result, including
attempt budgets, ledger and pending repair. It does not execute a stage again,
open the preserved journals for repair, or send another signal. Repeated verify
must return the same observations. A hash, parse or replay mismatch is a stop,
not permission to rewrite the fixture to match its expected result.

For a real interrupted or uncertain run, follow
[stopped-writer inspection and run control](../operate.md#inspect-a-run) and
[pipeline state recovery](../recovery.md#pipeline-state-recovery). This helper
uses whole completed child outcomes; it does not demonstrate a crash between
acceptance and receipt or an external provider's reconciliation.

## Cleanup and change boundaries

After retaining the observations needed for your task:

```bash
node docs/site/use/workflows/examples/repair-retry.mjs cleanup "$REPAIR_REHEARSAL"
```

The helper checks its private ownership marker, absolute path, UID, selected
checkout and exact current HEAD before run, verify or cleanup. A changed HEAD
must reject before action: preserve the fixture and return to the original
selected source rather than rewriting its marker. Cleanup removes only that
owned fixture, including its disposable Git commits, copied plugins, run state,
artifact store and observations. It never changes the selected source checkout
or a real platform. A failed or unknown-ownership fixture requires its owner's
investigation, not an arbitrary recursive delete.

Change category limits, retry inputs or checker findings only in a new prepared
fixture before execution. Retain the old inputs and outcomes. For production
changes, use the [Core retry/repair contract](../../understand/nova-core.md#8-technical-retry-and-product-repair),
the original graph/package identities and the owning plugin's compatibility and
reconciliation procedure. A new budget does not amend the authority of an
already-pinned run.
